name: Field Drab
lede: Field Drab is a grayish yellowish brown from the ISCC-NBS 1955 color-name dictionary, one of sixteen names sharing its block.

sections.title: One of sixteen names in block 95
sections.body:
The ISCC-NBS circular of 1955 assigns this hue to block 80, naming the region grayish yellowish brown, Munsell notation 3.2Y 3.7/5.1 [1]. Wikipedia's entry for Field Drab cites the same circular [1]. A nearby block in the same dictionary, block 95, groups sixteen separate names together, among them Bison, Bracken, Butternut, Cocher and Siberian Brown, a reminder that the 1955 system named far more shades than any one word can now call to mind [2].

The nearest named colors on file are [[acanthe]], [[mud]], [[medal-bronze]] and [[bronze]], at 2.6, 4.4, 4.7 and 4.7 ΔE [2]. Field Drab sits between [[olive]] and [[khaki]], duller and darker than either [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of Field Drab covers at least five percent of the canvas in 2,155 of them, about 9.1 percent overall, the most common color discussed, as photographed [3]. Its rate is fairly steady from the 1600s to the 1800s, holding near or just above the archive average the whole span, with a brief peak in the 1440s [3]. Fritz Thomsen carries it most, in 11 of his 18 archived paintings, nearly seven times the average rate, and it most often appears alongside [[olive]] and [[brown]] [3].
